english:
We have already set forth, in our works, that the prophets sometimes present their prophecies in the form of parables[^1]; for it happens at times that (the prophet) sees a thing through a parable, and subsequently the meaning of the parable is explained to him in that same prophetic vision. It is as[^2] with a man who has a dream, and who, in that very dream, imagines that he has awakened, that he has related the dream to another, and that the latter has explained its meaning to him, whereas the whole was but a dream. This is what is called: 'a dream which has been interpreted in a dream[^3],' while there are also dreams whose meaning one knows after having awakened. Likewise, the meaning of prophetic parables is sometimes explained in the prophetic vision, as is evident with regard to Zechariah, who says, after having first presented certain parables: *And the angel that talked with me came again, and waked me, as a man that is wakened out of his sleep; and said unto me, What seest thou? etc.* (Zech. 4:1 and 2); then he (the angel) explains to him the (new) parable[^4].

[^1]: Literally: *that the prophets sometimes prophesy by parables*. See *Abridgment of the Talmud*, treatise *Yesôdé ha-Tôrâ*, ch. VII, § 3.—The Arabic mss. generally have תואליפנא, in the plural, *our works;* the Hebrew versions have, one בחבורנו, the other בספרנו, in the sing.
[^2]: In the editions of the version of Ibn-Tibbon, it is necessary to erase the word כי, and read only כמו, as the mss. have, and also Al-’Harîzi.
[^3]: See Babylonian Talmud, treatise *Berakhôth*, fol. 55 *b*.
[^4]: Zechariah, after having presented, in ch. I-III, several parables, relates in ch. IV a new vision which he had and which is presented by the parable of the candlestick with seven branches; then the meaning of this parable is explained to him by the angel in this same vision, first the general meaning and then the details (ch. IV, v. 6-14).

And this is likewise evident with regard to Daniel; for it is said first: *Daniel saw a dream, and visions of his head upon his bed* (Dan. 8:1); and after having related all the parables and having expressed how greatly he was distressed at not knowing the explanation thereof, he finally interrogates the angel, and the latter makes known to him the explanation, in that same vision: *I came near*, he says, *unto one of them that stood by, and asked him the truth of all this. So he told me, and made me know the interpretation of the things* (ibid., v. 16). After having said that he *saw a dream*, he calls the whole event ’HAZÔN (a vision), because, as he says, it was an angel who explained it to him in a prophetic dream. He says therefore, after that: *A vision* (’HAZÔN) *appeared unto me, even unto me Daniel, after that which appeared unto me at the first* (ibid., 8:1). This is clear[^1]; for ’HAZÔN is derived from the verb ’HAZA, as MAREA (vision) is derived from RAA, and the two verbs have the same meaning (that of *seeing*), so that there is no difference between the words MAREA, MA’HAZÉ and ’HAZÔN. There is no third way (of prophecy) besides these two ways of which the Pentateuch speaks: *I will make myself known unto him in a* VISION, *and will speak unto him in a* DREAM (Num. 12:6)[^2]; but there are in this gradations, as shall be explained[^3].

[^1]: That is to say: it is clear that it is here a question of a *vision*, designated by the word ’HAZÔN.
[^2]: The author intends to say that the word ’HAZÔN (חזון) cannot indicate a third way of prophetic inspiration, and it is necessarily synonymous with MAREA (מראה) and MA’HAZÉ (מחזה).
[^3]: See hereafter, ch. XLV.

— Nevertheless, among the prophetic parables, there are also many whose meaning is not at all explained in the prophetic vision, but whose intention the prophet knows after having awakened, as is the case, for example, with the *staves* which Zechariah took in a prophetic vision[^1].

[^1]: See Zechariah, ch. 11, v. 7 and following. The meaning of this parable was not at all explained to the prophet in his vision, as was that of the *candlestick*, mentioned above. Our author himself attempts further on to indicate its meaning.

It must be known that, just as the prophets see things which have a parabolic meaning,—as, for example, the *lamps* of Zechariah (Zech. 4:2), the *horses* and the *mountains* (ibid., 6:1-7), the *roll* of Ezekiel (2:9), the *wall* made by a *plumb-line* which Amos saw[^1] (7:7), the *beasts* which Daniel saw (ch. 7 and 8), the *seething pot* which Jeremiah saw (1:13), and other similar parables, by which it is intended to trace certain ideas,—so also they see things by which it is intended (to indicate) what the *name* of the thing seen recalls by its etymology or by its homonymy, in such a manner that the action of the imaginative faculty consists, as it were, in making one see a thing bearing a homonymous name, by one of the significations of which one is guided toward another, which also is one of the species of allegory[^2]. When, for example, Jeremiah says: (that he saw) MAKKEL SCHAKED, *a rod of an almond tree*, his intention is to deduce (something) from the homonymy of the word SCHAKED[^3], and he says afterward: *For I am* SCHÔKED, *vigilant, etc.* (Jer. 1:11 and 12); for it is a question neither of the idea of the *rod*, nor of that of the *almond tree*. Likewise, when Amos sees KELOUB KAÏÇ, *a basket of summer fruit*, it is to deduce therefrom the fulfillment of the time; and he says: For *the* KÈÇ (or *the end*) *is come* (Amos 8:2).

[^1]: Almost all the mss. bear: אלדׄי ראה; the word ראה must be pronounced رَأَى; it would have been more correct to say אלתי ראהא, the word חומה being feminine; but perhaps the author thought of the masculine word אנך, or of a masculine Arabic word such as حائط or تمور, *wall*. The ms. of the Hebrew supplement of the Imperial Library, no. 63, written by the hand of R. Saadia Ibn Danan, bears אלתי ראה.
[^2]: In other words: The prophets sometimes see things which do not represent by themselves an allegorical subject, but whose name only recalls, by its etymology, a certain idea which is expressed by a similar name, so that the whole vision is founded only on a play on words, as the author is about to explain by some examples.
[^3]: That is to say, to play upon the double meaning of the root שקד, from which are derived at once the word which signifies *almond tree*, and that which signifies *vigilant, attentive*, so that the vision of *the almond tree* indicates these words of God: *for I am vigilant to perform my word*. Cf. above, ch. XXIX, p. 229, and ibid., note 2.

— What is yet more astonishing is when attention is awakened by means of a certain name whose letters are also those of another name, in an inverted order[^1], although there be between these two names no etymological relation, nor any community of meaning, as is found (for example) in the parables of Zechariah, when, in a prophetic vision, he takes the two *staves*[^2] for feeding the flock and gives to one the name of NO’AM (grace, favor) and to the other, that of ’HÔBELÎM (destroyers)[^3]. In this parable, it is intended (to indicate): that the nation, in its primitive state, enjoyed the *favor of the Eternal* who guided and directed it, that it was joyful in obeying God and felt pleasure therein[^4], and that God was propitious to it and loved it—[as it is said: *Thou hast this day exalted the Eternal etc. and the Eternal hath exalted thee etc.* (Deut. 26:17 and 18)[^5]]—when it was guided and directed by Moses and by the Prophets who succeeded him; but that afterward it changed so much in disposition that it held in aversion obedience to God, so that God held it in aversion and made of its leaders *destroyers*, like Jeroboam and Manasseh. Such (is the meaning) according to the etymology; for ’HÔBELÎM (חובלים) is of (the same root as) ME’HABBELÎM, מחבלים כרמים (*that* DESTROY *the vines*, Song of Sol. 2:15). Then, he deduces equally therefrom,—I mean from the name of ’HÔBELÎM,—that they held in *aversion* the Law and that God held them in aversion. But this meaning can only be derived from ’HÔBELÎM by means of the transposition of the letters ’H, B, L; he says therefore, with regard to the idea of *aversion* and *abomination* which this parable contains: *My soul was withdrawn from them*[^6] *and their soul also had an aversion* (BA’HALA) *for me* (Zech. 11:8), and he transposes the letters ’H B L (חבל) to make of them B ’H L (בחל).

[^1]: That is to say, when the prophet, to make allusion to a certain subject, makes use of a name which, by itself, has an entirely different meaning, but whose transposed letters give the name of the subject in question.
